description: we aim to create an VR, AI supported, engaging, interactive learning experience that helps young explorers think and act like astronauts. Through playful missions and hands-on challenges, we want to spark curiosity about space while encouraging problem-solving, teamwork, and scientific thinking.
summary: Sarmad: First Light is a free 3D browser mission that trains children aged 7-12 to think like junior astronauts. The player is the junior systems officer of Majan Station, a small outpost near Shackleton crater on the Moon, after a power fault. In six short scenes they share a few power units between life support, crop lights and a rover, move the crew into a covered shelter when a solar particle alert arrives, and plan a three-turn recovery. No choice is free: shelter postpones a surface sample, and a faster repair pauses the crop lights once. The alert comes from a real, archived NASA DONKI record (a solar energetic particle event on 10 May 2024), shown with its date, ID and instrument and never presented as live. After guided practice, the child solves fresh tasks without hints, and the mission report shows a teacher or parent each of the three skills separately. It turns real mission trade-offs (power, radiation shelter, food, communication delay) into a short, replayable decision loop a young child can follow. It runs in any modern browser with mouse, touch or keyboard, No download, no account.
details:
What it does

- A single lunar episode, "First Light", of about 20 minutes, for ages 7-12 in a classroom, club or at home, with an adult facilitator if possible.

- Three learning outcomes from our instructional design (Sarmad Instructional Design v1.1, written by the team):

1. Share limited power: life support first, crop lights, rover charge; the total must fit the supply.

2. Shelter the crew: use thick cover and a route that can be reached in time, not shade or a "force field".

3. Plan the recovery: charge the rover battery, repair, and turn the crop lights back on within three turns.

- Six scenes: airlock and mission briefing (with a warm-up), power station, shelter map, recovery plan (with a message delay to Mission Control Muscat, then a short practice drive), "your own turn" (fresh tasks, no hints), mission report. The top bar shows "Step n of 6", the steps done and the steps left. There is no timer race.

- Rover drive (a short practice drive, not scored): after the recovery plan, the child drives the repaired rover to the surface sample the crew had to postpone and brings it back to the shelter. The battery is the number of power units the child gave the rover in their own plan. On the way, a training alert ("not a real warning", like the archived solar event) gives them 10 seconds to drive into a cover ring and 4 seconds to wait there. If the battery runs out or the rover is not in cover in time, a short lesson says why and the child can retry (a retry starts with 6 units). Arrow keys, W A S D or on-screen arrow buttons, in 3D and in the flat 2D view. The screen says "Training route, not a real map. Practice only: nothing here is scored.", and a "Skip drive" button is always there.

- On phones and in the flat view: the power-sharing +/- buttons fit without scrolling, the flat-version note can be closed, and the 3D drive labels Cover, Shelter and Sample with an arrow to the sample when it is off screen and keeps the rover and labels in the free view between the battery bar and the arrow buttons; the battery reads "Battery left: n of m units" in 3D and flat.

- The result of each decision comes first: after Confirm, "What your choice did" gives one line each for power, life support, radiation protection and food production, then why, and what it cost.

- Short story intros, so children act sooner; the rules and "Hear it again" stay available.

- A lighter planning screen: a short rule card on top ("All rules" opens the full card), the active turn framed in gold, the power left shown for each turn, and "Same as turn n" to copy a turn and save taps.

- Clear controls: a short hint right above the controls of each step, and a clear "chosen" look (filled, bold, with a diamond).

- "Your own turn" works in the flat 2D view as well as in 3D: the task card, the answer controls and Submit appear right away, Submit asks once to confirm, and "Stop here" lets a child finish early (the rest is marked "not assessed"). The game never fills in answers for the child here.

- Every choice has a cost. Shelter keeps the crew safe but the surface sample waits. A fast repair costs one crop-light pause, a slow repair costs time. Wrong plans are not punished: the game names the rule that was broken and why, and the child tries again.

- Communication delay: a status message to Mission Control Muscat takes a labelled 5 seconds one way, with a countdown on screen (a teaching example; the Science & Sources page says real Moon links take about 3 to 14 seconds), so the crew uses the rule card on board while they wait.

- Updated after a usability session: on 15 November our team lead and three children played the hosted site and told us what was unclear. The changes above (result first, shorter intros, step counter, lighter planning screen, clearer controls, "Your own turn" in the flat view, the practice drive) answer that feedback. This was usability feedback from one session, not a learning study.

How it works

- NASA data is the trigger of a decision. The bundled DONKI record 2024-05-10T13:35:00-SEP-001 (GOES-P: SEISS >10 MeV) opens the shelter decision. The in-game source card shows the event date, ID, instrument and an ARCHIVED label, with a link to the record. The record ID is carried into the mission report and the facilitator view.

- "Play again" can load a different real archived event from a bundled snapshot of DONKI SEP records (19 Nov 2025 to 14 Nov 2026; only the 20 observed records are offered, model runs are skipped), so replays vary while staying real. The snapshot is bundled with the game; nothing is fetched live.

- Honest science: date, ID and instrument are read from the NASA record. Power units, route minutes, cover labels and the drive's training route are teaching rules, and the game says so. It never gives a dose, a forecast or a safe time outside.

- Evidence of learning comes from committed decisions, not clicks or speed. Each outcome gets its own result: met independently, met with support, needs practice, or not assessed. The practice drive is not part of the evidence. Evidence stays in the browser tab: anonymous, no names, no account. A facilitator view (key F9 or the pause menu) shows the evidence table and data provenance and can export it as JSON.

- Accessibility: spoken narration of the scene instructions with captions (the practice drive and the result lines are on-screen text), the rule cards of "Your own turn" read aloud with their numbers ("Hear it again", key R, repeats them), large targets, full keyboard play, touch, a 2D view when WebGL is off, sound on/off, less motion.

- Omani setting as a cultural bridge: Mission Control Muscat, Majan Station, the crew Engineer Hamad and Dr. Muna, CapCom Salma, a date-palm seedling in the crop rack, a shelter that "feels like a majlis", Omani geometric patterns and a star wall in honour of the navigator Ahmad ibn Majid. All fictional; not affiliated with or endorsed by NASA.

Benefits and goals

- Turns real mission trade-offs (power, shelter, food, delay) into a short, replayable decision loop that a 7-year-old can follow, and shows a teacher what each child could do.

- Next (not yet built): a small pilot with children in both age bands (no learning data has been collected yet, so no learning gains are claimed), a science review by specialists, and future work on VR, an AI ground assistant, multiplayer, an Arabic interface and new 3D environments.

Tools and languages

- JavaScript (ES modules), HTML5, CSS, three.js 0.187 (MIT), WebGL; static site, no server code, no calls to NASA or any other server at run time, no API key. Node.js for tests and the build. Blender for 3D models, FFmpeg for audio and video.

- Testing: 344 automated unit tests, scripted plays of every valid plan and every kind of rejected plan, and real-input play in Chrome with mouse and keyboard, and with touch at tablet and phone sizes (touch emulated in Chrome). The shipped build was played to the end in 3D at 1280x720 with the mouse and with touch at 390x844 and 844x390. The only recorded real-device play is the team's usability session (older build).
